meta.title: Use of Mortar and Pestle in Pharmacognosy Laboratory

sections.purpose: To manually grind, triturate, and reduce the particle size of crude drugs, plant materials, and chemical reagents for phytochemical screening, extract preparation, and microscopic examination.
sections.scope: Applicable to Pharmacognosy laboratory for small-scale grinding of crude drugs, preparation of aqueous suspensions, and maceration of fresh plant material.
procedure: Select the appropriate mortar and pestle type: porcelain for general grinding; agate or glass for fine pharmaceutical work; stone (granite) for heavy grinding of hard materials; brass for traditional preparation.
Inspect the mortar and pestle for cracks, chips, or residue from previous use before starting.
Clean with a damp cloth or rinse with the same solvent to be used in the experiment — dry thoroughly.
Cut or break the crude drug material into small pieces (< 1 cm) before placing in the mortar to reduce grinding effort.
Place a small quantity of the drug in the mortar — do not overfill (fill to < 1/3 capacity).
Grip the pestle firmly and apply downward pressure combined with a circular rotating motion.
Grind steadily and systematically — after every 2–3 rotations, use a spatula to push material from the sides to the centre.
Sieve the ground material periodically through the target mesh sieve; return any coarse fraction to the mortar for further grinding.
For wet grinding (preparation of extracts for phytochemical tests): add the extraction solvent in small portions while grinding.
After grinding, collect all material, label, and transfer to a suitable container.
Clean the mortar and pestle: rinse with the used solvent; wash with soap and water; dry completely before storage.
For highly aromatic or coloured drugs (turmeric, saffron), clean with ethanol before washing with water.
Record material name, quantity, grinding method, and target particle size in the logbook.
precautions: Wear a dust mask when grinding fine or aromatic powders — airborne drug dust can cause respiratory sensitization.
Do not grind strongly corrosive chemicals (concentrated acids/bases) in porcelain mortars — corrosion contaminates subsequent samples.
Never grind reactive combinations (e.g., oxidizers with organic material) together — risk of explosion or fire.
Handle agate and glass mortars with care — they are brittle and expensive.
Dedicate separate mortars for: aromatic drugs (retain odour), coloured drugs (staining), toxic plants — label clearly.
Wet the mortar lightly with solvent before grinding hygroscopic materials to prevent electrostatic loss of fine powder.
Do not use chipped or cracked mortars — sharp edges and contamination from mortar material affect results.
